Need coronary vasospasm provocation testing (e.g., acetylcholine or ergonovine) or cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement to distinguish vasospasm from myocarditis, as these are the core confirmatory tests for the leading hypothesis.

Need results of intracoronary acetylcholine/ergonovine provocation testing and cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement to confirm alcohol-induced coronary vasospasm versus myocarditis; also request serum ethanol level and continuous ECG recording during a spontaneous post-alcohol episode to establish the temporal trigger.

bindings.label: Patient in their 50s presented with recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol
Symptoms persisted for 2 years and worsened on admission; episodes usually occurred 6-20 hours after alcohol ingestion and lasted 5-10 minutes; syncope occurred only after large alcohol intake
Past medical history included hypertension diagnosed 3 months prior
Social history included smoking and alcohol overconsumption (250g/week) for about 20 years
Physical examination documented no specific findings
ECG reveals high-degree AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and widespread ST elevations
Laboratory tests show normal troponin and potassium
Blood alcohol, glucose, lactate, ketones, and liver function tests were not obtained
Patient has acute coronary syndrome or myocarditis
Coronary angiography reveals only mild stenosis
Patient has myocarditis or coronary vasospasm
ECG shows transient widespread ST elevations
Alcohol is a recognized trigger of coronary vasospasm
Cardiac MRI, endomyocardial biopsy, and vasospasm provocation testing have not been performed
